title: The Afternoon Brief: Courts, disasters and deportations mark a heavy Sunday
dek: A federal judge blocked deportations over speech on Israel, Nepal's flood toll climbed past 780, a Cyprus ferry capsized, and Iceland voted against reopening EU talks, while the White House's Venezuela oil deal and a teleprompter operator's insider-trading fine carried over from Friday.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: The day's disparate stories share a common test: rules and limits, legal, natural and regulatory, meeting figures who expected exceptions.
bottom_line: Sunday's stories, from a blocked deportation policy to a fined White House aide to a deported deportation advocate, shared a pattern of rules catching up with actors who expected exceptions, while Nepal's flood toll climbed to 788 dead and 2,502 missing and a Cyprus ferry capsizing added at least 7 deaths with 24 still missing. Iceland's voters rejected resuming EU talks by a narrow margin on record turnout, and Michigan's Senate race saw a contested apology over synagogue-attack remarks. The reporting is solid on what regulators and courts found and ordered but leaves unresolved the legal fate of the Venezuela oil deal and the causes behind the Aarau and Trenton shootings. Watch for a possible Lindell appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court, any Venezuelan legal challenge to the oil agreement, and updated missing-person figures from Nepal and Cyprus in the coming days.
body: The throughline connecting Sunday's stories is enforcement catching up with people and governments who assumed they were exempt from it. A federal judge blocked the Trump administration from deporting noncitizen students over speech critical of Israel. A commentator who spent years demanding aggressive deportation was himself deported for overstaying his visa. A White House teleprompter operator who traded on advance knowledge of the president's own speeches was fined. And Iceland's voters, weighing sovereignty against security, said no to reopening a negotiation their government wanted revived.

Overseas, the day's heaviest news was casualty count. Nepal's flood death toll reached 788 with 2,502 people still missing, according to CBS News reporting cited in the day's coverage, after a glacial bedrock collapse in the Himalayan region triggered flash floods on Wednesday; Chinese authorities reported 16 dead and 546 missing on their side of the border. Fresh flood warnings on the Bhotekoshi River forced repeated evacuations Sunday, a compounding crisis for a population already displaced. Separately, a ferry carrying nearly 270 passengers capsized off northern Cyprus, killing at least 7 people, with 237 rescued and 24 still missing; the vessel began taking on water roughly 15 minutes after departing Kyrenia for the Turkish port of Tasucu. In Switzerland, a shooting at a rave in Aarau killed a 22-year-old woman and wounded five others, with the shooter still at large and a cross-border manhunt underway with German authorities. In Trenton, New Jersey, a shooting at a block party killed two people and wounded eight others, with more than 50 spent shell casings recovered and no arrests announced.

On the legal and political front, U.S. District Judge Noël Wise ruled Friday that the administration's practice of threatening to deport noncitizen students over speech critical of Israel violated the First and Fifth Amendments, in a lawsuit brought by The Stanford Daily. The same weekend brought two versions of the Milo Yiannopoulos deportation story: he was arrested by ICE at New Orleans airport on August 27 and deported to the UK on either August 28 or August 29 depending on the account, after failing to appear for an immigration hearing that produced a final removal order on July 22. The Department of Homeland Security said he 'chose to overstay his welcome,' and the administration publicized the case alongside its voluntary self-deportation program. In Minnesota, the state Supreme Court rejected Mike Lindell's bid to force a full recount of the Republican gubernatorial primary he lost to Lisa Demuth, with Chief Justice Natalie E. Hudson writing that Lindell's claim "confused the purpose of a manual recount with an election contest"; Lindell has said he will appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court.

In Michigan, Democratic Senate nominee Abdul el Sayed apologized to the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus for a March statement responding to a synagogue attack, saying "if my statement caused pain, I'm sorry." Republican nominee Mike Rogers rejected the apology as "too little, too late." And in Iceland, voters rejected resuming EU accession talks 52.8% to 47.2%, on turnout of 82.5%, the highest since 2009, a result tied to fishing rights concerns even as Arctic security tensions framed the campaign.

Carrying over from Friday, the administration's announced Venezuela oil agreement, granting the U.S. majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of proven reserves, remains without a published text, and the BBC has reported it is unclear whether the arrangement could face legal and constitutional challenges in Venezuela. Also carrying over, the CFTC's fine against Gabriel Perez, the White House teleprompter operator who profited roughly $107,500 betting on the content of Trump's speeches, was finalized at $172,000 combined, with a three-year trading ban; federal prosecutors in Manhattan declined to open a criminal case, according to ABC News reporting.

The reporting does not explain why the Nepal and Cyprus disasters intensified this weekend beyond the mechanics described, glacial collapse and rapid water intake, nor does it establish a motive in either the Swiss or Trenton shootings. On Iceland's vote, the stories describe fishing rights and sovereignty as dominant themes without a stated single decisive factor.

Desk boards were unavailable this cycle, so the figures above rest on the day's stories as reported, with historical framing where two versions of a story diverge, as in the Yiannopoulos deportation date.

The coming days will test several open threads: whether Venezuela's government or courts challenge the oil agreement's legal standing, whether the Justice Department appeals Judge Wise's ruling and how broadly it applies, whether Lindell's promised Supreme Court appeal is filed, whether Nepal and Chinese authorities report updated casualty figures as the search for thousands of missing continues, and whether investigators in Aarau or Trenton identify suspects.
